authoredFrom: code and two runs: the claim shape was observed in a token issued by better-auth 1.6.26 and verified from a Cloudflare Worker (agentpod#331), and the control pair moved from reserved to issued when grants became data the issuer can read (principal_grants); `act` added 2026-08-30 when the Application Service gained the ability to assert a human it had never met, on the strength of a Matrix message and a principal_identities row; `mayDispatch` became bare `prn_…` ids matched by equality on 2026-08-30, when an agent became a principal and the two namespaced, pattern-matched forms were deleted rather than deprecated (charter decisions/2026-08-30-an-agent-is-a-principal.md §3); `email`/`email_verified` added 2026-09-20 (agentpod `apps/hub/src/auth/jwt-claims.ts`, `buildTokenPayload`'s conditional spread, and the join it reads from in `apps/hub/src/services/principals.ts`) so superpipeline can resolve or create a local user from a hub token instead of only verifying it carries a real, unnamed principal — part of the suite sign-in programme, task 1 of 2026-09-20-suite-sign-in
purpose: One issuer, and every other plane verifies offline against a JWKS (charter decisions/2026-08-15-one-issuer-and-offline-verification.md). The moment a second plane reads a claim, the claim's NAME is a contract: a rename in the hub is a silent authorization failure in superpipeline, which fails in the direction that looks like the caller having no permission. This corpus is what makes that a failing test instead.

howToRead.issued: Claims the issuer MUST put in every token, and consumers may rely on. A missing one is a malformed token. NOTE the difference between a claim that is ABSENT and one that is EMPTY: absent means this issuer does not speak the control pair, empty (`[]` / `false`) means this principal is permitted nothing. Reading the first as the second would let an old issuer silently authorise everything.
howToRead.standard: Registered JWT claims the issuer sets. Consumers MUST validate iss, aud and exp.
howToRead.reserved: Names that are SPOKEN FOR and not yet issued. A token must not use them to mean anything else, and a consumer must not infer permission from their absence.
howToRead.reject: Tokens a consumer MUST refuse. These are the point of the corpus — a fixture of only-valid examples proves almost nothing.
howToRead.conditional: Claims present only on SOME tokens. A consumer must not require them, and must not read their absence as a weaker caller — absence is the ordinary case.

algorithm.source: observed in agentpod#331; better-auth's jwt plugin default
algorithm.note: Consumers MUST pin the algorithm rather than trusting the token header, or a token signed with `alg: none` — or with a key of the consumer's choosing — is accepted.

issued.meaning: The principal acting. Today this is the Better Auth user id in AgentPod's hub; when the Organization plane mints principals it becomes that id, and this corpus changes with it.

What kind of principal `sub` names. Present because this suite exists to make humans and agents both first-class — a consumer that cannot tell them apart cannot enforce separation of duties, which is what charter decisions/2026-08-14-approvals-cross-planes-as-events.md turns on.

AgentPod's local isolation boundary for this principal. NOT the organisation: the organisation is owned by the Organization plane and recorded on each product's tenant as an optional external mapping (agentpod migration 0036, superpipeline migration 0002).

First half of the control pair — which agents this principal may dispatch. Values are bare principal ids, matched by EQUALITY. A grant no longer names an agent per plane with a namespaced pattern; it enumerates the `prn_…` ids of the agents it covers.

valueRules.equality: A value matches a principal id if and only if it is that id, character for character. There is no pattern language: `*` is not a wildcard here, it is a string that will never equal a real id. Patterns were deleted, not deprecated, because they matched things nobody intended — `hermes:*` silently spanned nodes, and `agentpod:*/hermes` reached a root station that should never have existed and was removed on 2026-08-30.
valueRules.unrecognisedIsIgnored: A consumer IGNORES a value that is not a `prn_…` id; it must never deny on one. A claim is read by more planes over time, and a plane that refused what it did not understand would break the day a third one appeared. The `prn_` prefix is the namespace now, so 'ignore an unrecognised value, never deny it' keeps working with no separate namespace grammar to check it against.
valueRules.emptyDenies: `[]` is a decision, and the decision is no. It is what an operator writes to suspend someone without deleting their grant.
valueRules.unassignedStationIsNobodys: A station occupied by no principal has no id to enumerate, so no grant can name it — it is dispatchable by nobody. That is a behaviour change from the per-plane, wildcard-bearing form this claim used to carry.

issued.meaning: Second half of the control pair — whether this principal may grant an agent its reach. Both halves are required: dispatch control alone is decorative, because anyone who can grant an agent production credentials does not need permission to dispatch it.

standard.meaning: The issuer's base URL. Consumers MUST validate it.
Expiry. THE REVOCATION SLA: agentpod#331 proved a token issued before a session is revoked keeps verifying until it expires, because verification is offline by design.

reject.why: A token with `alg: none` carries no signature. Pin the algorithm; never take it from the header.
exp in the past. This is the whole revocation story — a consumer that ignores exp has no revocation at all.
A validly signed token from another issuer is still not ours.
A token minted for a different audience must not be replayable here.

Signed by a key not in the JWKS — including a key that WAS in it and has been retired. agentpod#331 found retirement propagates only as fast as each consumer's JWKS cache, so this case is reachable in normal operation, not only under attack.
A token that verifies but names no tenant is not a weaker caller, it is an unresolvable one. Refuse it rather than falling back to a default boundary.

A token from an issuer that predates the control pair. A consumer must not treat absence as an empty grant, nor as an unrestricted one — it means the issuer cannot answer, and the consumer decides its own posture.

`*` or `prn_*` in mayDispatch. Patterns were deleted on 2026-08-30, not deprecated: a grant is now an enumeration of principal ids, matched by equality, and a wildcard string simply fails that check — it must never be read as 'every agent' or 'every agent of this shape'. `agentpod:*/hermes` reaching a root station that should never have existed is the evidence this removal answers.

shape.sub: string — the service that minted this token

conditional.meaning: RFC 8693's actor claim. Present when a SERVICE minted this token while asserting a principal who was not present to sign in — today, the Matrix Application Service resolving an approval gate on behalf of the human who tapped a button in a room. `sub` remains the human; `act.sub` is who spoke for them.
conditional.whyItExists: charter decisions/2026-08-14-approvals-cross-planes-as-events.md requires a human's approval to reach superpipeline AS that human, because a bridge substituting its own identity would make every approval in the suite attribute to one account and void the separation-of-duties check. That requirement creates a token nobody signed in for. Such a token should not be INDISTINGUISHABLE from one a person minted from their own session — delegation that cannot be seen in the record is impersonation with better manners.
conditional.consumerObligation: A consumer MUST NOT grant more because `act` is present, and MUST NOT deny because it is absent. It carries no authority of its own: the claims beside it are built by the same code path a session token uses, so an assertion can never carry reach the person's own token would not. What a consumer MAY do is RECORD it, so an audit can distinguish 'she approved it' from 'the bridge approved it for her'.
conditional.signedBy: A separate key from the one session tokens use — agentpod migration 0054. Both are published in the same JWKS and verify identically, so this is an authority boundary rather than a cryptographic one: revoking the bridge's ability to speak for people is deleting one row, and does not sign every human out of the console.

conditional.meaning: The Better Auth email of the user linked to `sub`. Present only when the principal has one linked — absent, not present-and-null, for an agent or a service principal, or a human principal not yet linked to a Better Auth user. Always present together with `email_verified`; never one without the other.
conditional.whyItExists: superpipeline is the suite's second identity consumer and verifies hub tokens entirely offline. Before this claim it could confirm a token was authentic but could not learn who the person was — it could not match them to an existing local user, and could not create one either, since superpipeline's `users.email` column is `NOT NULL UNIQUE`. The OIDC standard spelling, not a bespoke name, is deliberate: it moves the token towards a conforming ID token a standard library can read, rather than a shape only this suite understands.
conditional.consumerObligation: MUST NOT be required, and MUST NOT read its absence as a weaker caller — an agent token asserting no email is the ordinary case, not a gap. A consumer resolving or creating a local user from this claim MUST also check `email_verified` before trusting the address as a matching key.

conditional.meaning: Whether the `email` claim above has been verified. Present exactly when `email` is present, and set to `false` for an unverified address rather than omitted — omitting it for an unverified address would read as 'no opinion', which is not what an unverified address means.
conditional.whyItExists: Same reason `email` exists: a consumer that matches or creates a local user from an address needs to know whether to trust it first.
conditional.consumerObligation: MUST NOT treat its absence as either 'verified' or 'unverified' — absence means `email` itself is absent, nothing more. When present, a consumer MUST gate anything that depends on the address being real (matching an existing account by it, for instance) on this being `true`.
